title: Verifiable immunization records across borders: the policy-maker track
description: The seven modules (M1 to M7) of the DPI-H workshop's policy-maker track, taught from the journeys J1 to J4.1 of one cross-border family: domestic and cross-border verifiable immunization records as the entry point to a personal health record. Converted from the VaxLink walkthrough's policyData.ts (scratch proof).
audience: Ministry of Health policy makers and digital health leads, at tables of one country each
promise: You will not leave with an assessment or a plan. You will leave knowing what each consists of, where your country stands on its first page, and who you would do the rest with.
useCaseStatement: A child vaccinated in ___ should be able to ___ in ___.

modules.title: From journey to capabilities
modules.carries: What had to exist for this moment to work — and where does our version of the journey break?
objectives: Name the capabilities each moment of the journey needs
Say where your country's version of the journey breaks
Choose a substitution pattern that gets you moving

modules.title: The reference architecture and where you stand
modules.carries: Which system do we use today for each block — and is it there, partly there, or absent?

modules.title: Standards, specifications and the core data set
modules.carries: Which standards do we adopt rather than author — and who owns the national core data set?

modules.title: Trust, credentials and wallets
modules.carries: Who signs, who verifies, and who would hold the national trust anchor? Name it; do not decide it.

modules.title: Governance, decision rights and the legal basis
modules.carries: Who holds each decision — and what legal basis lets the record cross a border and be shared for a child?
objectives: Name who holds each of the four decision rights today
Name the legal basis that lets a record cross a border and be shared for a child

modules.title: Doing it once, together
modules.carries: Would your neighbour need this too? If yes, why would you each build it?

modules.title: Our first move, what it costs, and what we ask for
modules.carries: What is realistic in twelve months with the people and money we have — and who owns it?
objectives: Write a realistic twelve-month first move with a named owner
Name the cost driver that dominates it

tables.title: Decision rights
tables.description: The four decision rights the use case forces.

rows.label: Architecture authority
rows.question: Who decides which national systems play which part, and that they must connect?

rows.label: Standards mandate
rows.question: Who can require suppliers to conform to the national implementation guide — in a tender, for example?

rows.label: Core data set custodian
rows.question: Who owns the national core data set, its codes and its mappings to other countries’ codes?

rows.label: Trust anchor
rows.question: Which institution signs on behalf of the health sector, and who accepts a foreign signature?

rows.label: Consent, including for minors and dependants

tables.title: Substitution patterns
tables.description: Taught at the end of M1 and reused all workshop.

rows.label: Start narrow
rows.what: One population, one credential, one facility type.

rows.label: Start shared
rows.what: Build the foundation once for several programmes, not once for immunization.
rows.example: Taifafeki’s registry shared across parts of government

rows.label: Start borrowed
rows.what: Adopt a regional or international artefact rather than authoring your own.
rows.example: The ICVP IG, the IPS, a SNOMED subset

rows.label: Devices and connectivity at the point of care
Recurrent cost of running shared infrastructure
The cost of not doing it once

steps.askTheRoom: What is the minimum a family should leave hospital with when their baby has no national ID?
steps.facilitatorCue: Start with Khamla, not the technology. Hold up a paper card: this is the only thing that crosses the border.

questions.text: Write your country’s use-case statement: “A child vaccinated in ___ should be able to ___ in ___.”
Who in your government would sign this card on behalf of the health sector: the hospital, the ministry, or a national trust service?
Does your law let a facility issue a health credential to a child who is not a citizen and has no national ID?

capabilities.label: A national service that signs vaccination certificates
An immunization record at the birth facility

tags.why: Issue to the WHO digital certificate specification rather than design a national card.

steps.askTheRoom: Is an “unverified but recorded” vaccine useful to the next clinician — or a risk?
steps.facilitatorCue: This is the key trust boundary in the story. Pause and make sure everyone sees why the CHW does not verify.

questions.text: Does your national core data set tell a dose the family reported from one that was verified? Who defines that element?
Who is allowed to verify a foreign credential: a health worker’s phone, a clinic, or only a national service?

capabilities.label: A core data set that marks a dose as reported or verified

tags.why: Take the element from the WHO immunization core data dictionary rather than define it nationally.

steps.askTheRoom: Who should be allowed to create a health identity for a newborn — and how early?
steps.facilitatorCue: Ask who in the room has worked with CHWs. What does “offline” really mean in their context?

questions.text: Which block gives this child his first identifier in your country: birth registration, the national ID, or the health client registry? Exists, partial or absent?
When a birth happened abroad and is not registered at home, how does the child enter your registries — and your coverage denominator?
Who may create a health identity for a newborn at a home visit, and on whose consent?

capabilities.label: A client registry that can hold a child with no birth record
A link from birth registration (CRVS) to the health registries
An offline app for community health workers
A referral from the community to a facility

tags.why: One population first: newborns found in border districts.

steps.askTheRoom: When verification fails, what should the nurse do — and how is it explained to the family?
steps.facilitatorCue: Open the screen and flip the tamper toggle live. The contrast lands better than any explanation.

questions.text: What must be true for this nurse to trust a record she did not create?
Who would hold your national trust anchor, and who accepts a foreign signature on behalf of your health sector?
What must your country have, and what must it decide, before it can verify a neighbour’s card offline? Name it; do not decide it here.

capabilities.label: Membership of a trust network, its list cached for offline use

tags.why: The trust network is built once, for every programme that signs credentials, not for immunization alone.

steps.askTheRoom: Who should own the mapping between countries’ vaccine codes — WHO, each country, or each clinic?
steps.facilitatorCue: Emphasize: the Taifafeki record is never overwritten. Both codes live side by side.

questions.text: Who owns the national core data set and the mapping between other countries’ vaccine codes and yours?
Which code systems do you use for vaccine products, and is the licence question settled?
Would your neighbour need this mapping too? If yes, why would you each build it?

capabilities.label: A terminology service holding vaccine codes and mappings
The national schedule as computable decision logic

tags.why: Map to a shared regional or international code set rather than one country at a time.

steps.askTheRoom: How do we design for shared phones without compromising each person’s privacy?
steps.facilitatorCue: Notice Khamla’s mood dips here. Ask the room why — this is the equity tension in the story.

questions.text: Is a family wallet a national service, a private app, or both — and who decides which apps may hold a record?
Who may hold and share a child’s record: either parent, a guardian, the child from what age? What does your law say about dependants?

capabilities.label: A wallet or citizen app that holds a family’s records
Rules for a parent holding a child’s record

tags.why: One credential first: the child’s vaccination record, on the phone the family already has.

steps.askTheRoom: Is a 4-digit spoken passcode the right balance of security and ease for this family?
steps.facilitatorCue: Ask: what is inside this QR? (Answer: not the health data — just a pointer and a key.)

questions.text: What legal basis lets a record held at home be opened by a clinician abroad, on the family’s consent?
Would one clause in your procurement — conformance to the national IG — be enough for your portal to issue this link?
Who sets how a shared link is protected — the passcode, how long it lasts, who may open it: a national rule, or the family’s choice?
Should the part of the record that crosses borders (IPS plus an immunization core) be profiled once for the region, with national extensions left sovereign?

capabilities.label: A national health record the family’s link points to
A service that issues time-limited links on the family’s consent

tags.why: Adopt the IPS and an existing link specification rather than author a national format.

steps.askTheRoom: Should the family be notified every time their child’s record is viewed abroad?
steps.facilitatorCue: Close the loop: the story started and ends in Taifafeki. Ask what changed for each persona since step 1.

questions.text: What agreement makes every view abroad leave an entry in the home country’s log — and who reads it?
What would your country send to a regional connectathon within twelve months to prove this moment works?
What is a realistic twelve-month first move toward this moment, with a named owner — and which cost driver dominates it?

capabilities.label: A point-of-care viewer that accepts a foreign link
An access log kept in the home country

tags.why: Shared testing and one regional data model, rather than each pair of countries agreeing its own.

assessment.standingLine: “Absent” is a finding, not a failure — the question is only whether it blocks this use case.

discussion.question: How should national immunization systems handle temporary IDs for cross-border infants before civil registration is complete?
Why should offline CHW devices store foreign cards as “reported, not verified” rather than trying to verify them in the field?
When a monovalent vaccine is given abroad but the home schedule uses a combination (e.g. pentavalent), how should schedule rules calculate the doses still due?
What agreements do countries need so that a clinician viewing a record abroad triggers an audit entry back in the patient’s home country?

resources.title: Facilitator card: J4.1, crossing back
resources.body:
1. Show the QR on the family phone; say the passcode aloud.
2. Ask: *what is inside this QR?* (a pointer and a key, not the health data).
3. Try a wrong passcode: the attempt is still logged in Onesa.
4. Close the loop: ask what changed for each persona since J1.

presentation.story: Somsack is born in Taifafeki, grows up in Onesa, and one year later a Taifafeki doctor can see every vaccine he has ever had — without a single record being copied across the border.
presentation.lede: A baby and five people around him, four moments, twelve months. Follow the people first; the technology is what makes each hand-off possible.
presentation.presenterNote: Lead with people, not screens: introduce the cast, walk the four moments, then drop into a screen only when the room asks "what does that look like?"

about.title: This walkthrough is the demo of a FHIR implementation guide
about.text: The same journey is documented as a WHO SMART Guidelines DAK and FHIR IG: personas, business processes (BPMN), requirements, and every payload shown here as a published FHIR example.
